newsitem.title: USA: House lawmakers see support for new air standards.
newsitem.headline: House lawmakers see support for new air standards.

text.p: Three House members claimed Monday to have enough support to fend off efforts to delay or overturn the Environmental Protection Agency's controversial new clean air standards.

Reps. Henry Waxman, Democrat of California; Sherwood Boehlert, Republican of New York, and Christopher Shays, Republican of Connecticut, said more than 145 House colleagues had promised to back the strict new limits on smog and soot issued last month and due to come into effect within the next eight years.

"Even if legislation that would weaken the standards passed the House ... it would be impossible for opponents of the standards to override the president's veto," Waxman said in a statement. Opponents need at least 291 out of the 435 votes in the House to beat a veto.
"Once again, a bipartisan group has come together to ensure that we take the steps scientists tell us are necessary to protect human health and the environment," said Boehlert.

The battle lines over the new standards fall largely between regions, not parties, with northeastern states eager to see neighboring upwind states curb their pollution to help stop smog blowing into their area, while industrial states do not want to spend the money on new emissions cuts.
Republicans and industrial state Democrats vowed to pass a bill to put the new rules on hold, saying the tough health-based standards would cost billions of dollars to meet with little benefit.

Rep. John Dingell of Michigan, a powerful Democrat, was leading the fight against the clean air standards on the House side, saying air quality standards should not be tightened at a time when somes areas are struggling just to meet today's standards.

Despite concerns raised by local governments and industry groups about the costs of new pollution cuts, green groups were confident opponents will have a hard time securing enough votes, because any move to weaken the rules would be read as a vote against children's health and the environment.
The administration has said the stricter air quality standards will prevent 15,000 premature deaths a year and improve the health of thousands of children.
